The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)

I believe that in the Maritime provinces there are people who, owing to the almost depleted condition of the fisheries, would be willing to try their fortunes in western Canada if they were given some assistance by our Immigration department; but as matters stand to-day no native of this country who wishes to emigrate to the West can receive any such assistance. I think that provision should be made in connection with our immigration regulations that a man in eastern Canada who desires to try his fortunes in the West might be afforded some assistance in this direction. We have a's good a class of people in the Maritime provinces as can be found anywhere, and I know they would make good. I know that a large number of our men in eastern Canada are going to the United States just because they have nc-i the wherewithal to make a start in western Canada.
Another matter we look upon with suspicion is the Air Force. Is it really necessary for this country to spend $1,660,822 in experimenting with flying machines which have not yet proven of commercial value to the country? In the event of war, I venture to say that the experiments carried on in the United States and Great Britain will have provided means that will be ample to give us any information that we may stand in need of. We all hope that the day is far distant when flying machines for war purposes will be needed, and I submit that in the meantime such a heavy expenditure as this is not justifiable. I do not wish to be misunderstood; but we have heard a great deal about economy, and I have endeavoured in a brief way to indicate some instances in connection with which I believe that some measure of economy might welf be practised. In a return brought down in this House this year there appears some valuable information. This return is dated February 12, 1923, and gives the total number of employees in the inside Civil Service up to March 31, in each year from 1900 to 1922. The Civil Service Commission, I believe, is an institution that is growing away and beyond the dimensions ever dreamed of by its founders. I have no quarrel with the Civil Service, and I believe that the
11 p.m. Civil Service Commission is a body that is needed; but I do not believe that it can be defended in its present status. Do we realize that whereas in 1908 there were only five employees in the commission, to-day there are 220, and that in the former year while there was an expenditure of $4,329 today it is $342,000? I do not think it was ever the intention of any government of this coun-

try that this organization should attain such proportions. As I said before, immediately upon any branch of work being taken up, the commission as well as other branches of the government service begin to organize a staff and fortify themselves with officials; they entrench themselves in a position in which they think they will be secure. Now, in the evidence submitted to the committee inquiring into the Civil Service, Sir Joseph Pope, Under-Secretary of State, said-

I must draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that the rules of the House do not permit of reference to the evidence taken before any special committee before such committee's report has been submitted.

I regret the
transgression, Mr. Speaker; I will refrain from quoting the evidence. However, we know that a great deal of information has been gleaned which will be at the disposal of the House and of the public in a short time. Now, the different departments of government have greatly increased in cost, within recent years. The Department of Labour in 1910 had some 24 employees; in 1921 there were 105; and the increase in dollars and cents has been from $34,000 to $256,000. All along the line it is practically the same. I am glad to know, however, that since the present government has taken office there has been not only a reduction in the staff, but a large reduction in the expenditure of each department. In the Department of Justice there were 42 employees in 1900; to-day there are 208; and the cost was $36,000 then as compared with $270,000 now; and as I pointed out before, the number of employees in connection with the Civil Service Commission has increased from 5 in 1908 to 220 at the present time. The Department of External Affairs shows the same results. In the Department of the Interior, the Mines Branch, the number of employees has increased from 51 to 250, and the expenditure from $65,000 to $605,000. My object in submitting these figures is to show the tremendous cost of the expense of government in the different departments, which to the ordinary layman appears to be beyond all the necessities of these departments. I firmly believe that a reduction in the staff and in the cost of operation could be made in every direction. We have a great many committees in parliament, but I believe that we want an economy committee in this House to look carefully into the different departments and to submit a report, with a view to ascertaining whether

'The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
some saving cannot be effected in the directions I have suggested.
With regard to the Canadian National Railways, we believe in eastern Canada that there is already a decided improvement in the situation. The railway situation to which we took great exception regarding the management for the past few years has been greatly remedied in the past year. We in the Maritime provinces were united in our request that we should have more control and the eastern division placed back at Moncton. We are pleased that this has been done, and that Mr. L. S. Brown, one of the most competent railway officials in the entire service, has been placed in charge, with the result that already a great measure of relief has been given and a confidence restored that argues well for the future of the road.
Now in passing, just let me say that if our officials will realize the responsibility of theii positions and that the success of our railway lies largely in their hands, we may hope for a fair measure of success. I remember reading a motto that the owner of a railway had posted up in all his cars

"Courtesy costs nothing." It might be well for the officials of the Canadian National Railways to place a similar notice all over our system, as we are competing with a company that has given a great deal of attention to this phase of the operation of its lines.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the officials of the Canadian National Railways are not courteous?
No. I said at the outset-

Then I do not think the hon. gentleman should have expressed the opinion we have just listened to, because the experience of this House and of the people generally is that there is just as much courtesy on the Canadian National Railway as on any other line.

I quite agree with my hon. friend, but I do not think that a suggestion for even more courtesy will hurt. I think the success of our National Railways lies largely in the hands of the officials, and I have every confidence that they will not be lacking in courtesy; but, as I have said, courtesy costs nothing, and undoubtedly the travelling public demands it more and more.
I may be pardoned here if I make reference to a remark that appeared in the papers, attributed to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) to the effect that any concession that was obtained by the Crowsnest
pass agreement was forced on the government by the Progressive party. I wish to take exception to this remark. No one knows better than the hon. gentleman himself, who was a member of that committee, the true situation. He knows that it was due to the vote of the Liberals on that committee that they were enabled to obtain the relief that was given on the rates, not because they were forced by the hon. members of the Progressive party, but because they believed it was only fair and just that some relief should be given. I think if the hon. member made the remark attributed to him he owes this side of the House an apology, and I would be glad to give him the opportunity now of doing justice to the Liberals who assisted him and his colleagues on that occasion.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that this matter was brought to the attention of the House on a former occasion, and therefore I may be allowed now to offer a few words of explanation. During a sitting in camera of the Transportation Costs committee last session, after a Conservative member had spoken for some time explaining the change of ideas in regard to the Crowsnest pass arrangement, I whispered to him when he sat down-I was close beside him-"We forced you to it". I said this in a jocular tone, blit unfortunately his temper got the better of him, for he jumped to his feet and immediately announced what I had said. I think the member for Prince Edward Island was present, but he did not hear me make the remark, which was intended only for the ear of one gentleman. I hope there will be no further misunderstanding. It was an unfortunate remark and I admit I should not have made it, but it was made as an aside and never meant to go any further than that particular gentleman and would not have gone further if he had not lost his temper for the moment and spluttered it out to the whole gathering. That is the explanation I have to make of the incident referred to. In regard to giving credit to the Liberal members who assisted the Progressive members from the West on that occasion, I am prepared to make this statement on the floor of the House: During the recess at no time and in no place did I ever speak in connection with the Crowsnest pass agreement and what took place in committee and in this House without giving credit to the members of the Liberal party who stood by us at that time. Not only so, but I think I mentioned specifically three Liberal members-I cannot remember their constituencies for the moment-who stood
2972	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
with us all through and assisted in getting the matter brought before the members in such a way that they were inclined to support our motion.
I think the hon. gentleman is willing to admit that so far as I am concerned my stand on that committee was fair and above board.
Undoubtedly.

I thank the hon. gentleman for his explanation and I accept it in all good faith.
Last year in making a few observations on the budget I referred to the natural resources of the western provinces. We are still of the same mind in eastern Canada. We believe that we have an equity in the natural resources in the West, and we believe that when this matter is finally adjusted we shall receive just treatment. I could go into this matter more fully but I think sufficient has been placed on Hansard in the last few years to show that we have claims along these lines, and I have no doubt that the matter will be satisfactorily adjusted when the time comes.
As representing a farming community I wish to say that the farmers of our province have passed through just as trying a period possibly as the farmers of western Canada. We have been forced to take very low prices for our products, and transportation has been so high that it has been almost impossible to place our products on the market at a profit. However, we have a very industrious people and our farmers who take up diversified farming pay a great deal of attention to dairying, to the production of pork, eggs and different products of the farm that will find the best market we have, and in that way they are able .to tide over a period of depression such as we have experienced for the past few years. They are also endeavouring to put on the market the very best products that can possibly be produced, and I think it is up to the farmers of all Canada at this time to use their best endeavours along that line. The lower your market goes the better the product required and too much attention cannot be given by the farmers of this Dominion for putting our finished products on the market in the very best possible condition.
The matter of our fisheries has been taken up at greater length by other speakers than I propose to deal with it at the present time, although I am greatly interested in that industry. This year will be an exceedingly hard one for the fishermen on account of the late spring, which has made it impossible for

them to begin operations with the opening of the season, and unless some consideration is shown to them by extending the season this year there will be serious losses among them. I sincerely trust that when this matter comes before the cabinet later on in the season, the fishermen of eastern Canada will be given every consideration.
We talk about reciprocity with the United States, but I believe there is a reciprocity along other lines which we should try to develop. I believe we want great reciprocal or freer trade within our boundaries. If there [DOT] is one thing needed more than another it is the reduction of the cost of distribution from the factory to the farm, and from the farm to the factory. The city people need the products of the farm, and it is to the advantage of the farmer that he use his best endeavours to see that the man in the city gets the very best articles he can procure anywhere, and gets them at as low a cost as possible: that is, that the price be not doubled by the middleman.
Then again it is up to the manufacturer to see that his goods go to the farmer and labourer at the very lowest possible price. Cut out the middleman as much as possible, and let there be a freer trade between the consumer on the farm and the consumer in the city.
Let us get away from this idea of one trying to do the other for all he can, and let us get down to the essential truth that the more we can help one another the better it will be for all. Let us establish confidence in one another: get away from suspicion: do not try to set town against country, and country against town. One cannot exist without the other. Let us co-operate along the lines indicated, and I will venture the assertion that we have gone a long way to reduce the cost to each other, and at the same time give as much or more in return to the producers. Let us forget our differences and take each other into mutual confidence, and we have gone a long way towards a better understanding of each other's difficulties.
I think the evidence brought out in the special committee on agriculture will be very beneficial, and will give to the public more confidence in the business man and producer on the farm and in the factory.
I think that a great deal can be done along those lines to reduce the cost not only of manufactured articles to the man on the farm but also of farm products to the man in the city. I do not think any farmer will object to the city man getting his food products at the lowest possible price providing that the man

The Budget-Mr. Drummond
on the farm gets the highest market price that is going for his products.
Any criticism I have offered is offered with the best intention. I believe that a substantial saving can be made, and although personally I would have preferred very much to see a greater reduction in our customs tariff, still I feel that for the past two years we have accomplished something in tariff reduction, and I predict that notwithstanding what construction may be placed on the word "stability" in the Finance Minister's remarks, still the people of this country, especially the Liberal party, will demand a constant downward revision from year to year.
I am going to support the budget because the government showing is good. The deficits have been reduced from 674 million in 1920 to 47 million in 1923, and if it were not for the war burden left us, a surplus would have been shown-to say nothing of the railways.
I am going to support the budget because there has been an honest effort to reduce the tariff duties in the past two years, especially on the most important items, and to assist any industry that may start in Canada that all believe would be a benefit to us. I am going to support the budget because I believe the standing offer of reciprocal trade with the United States is a move in the right direction, and will yet be accepted by that country. You might as well try to keep the tide from coming in as to stop trade flowing in its natural courses. I am going to support the budget because I believe that out of his large parliamentary experience in dealing with the fiscal policy of this country, the Finance Minister believes that the budget as presented is the best in the interest of our people, having regard to our diversified industries and callings, and to our financial obligations.
I am going to support the budget in preference to the amendment because it contains now nearly all that is asked for in the amendment and proves conclusively that our Progressive friends are fast becoming adepts at playing politics. I am going to support the budget because the greatest era of prosperity in Canada was under Liberal rule and it will come again if we give Canada's Grand Old Man, the Minister of Finance, a fair trial in this critical period of our country's history.
In closing, I would say:	Let us have faith
in this great country of ours. We have the best laws of any country in the world. Our people observe those laws better than any people in the world. The observance of the seventh day as a day of rest, which is the bulwark of any nation, is better observed by Canada than any other country in the woild. We have the richest country in the world in
natural resources in comparison with our population. We have open ports on the Atlantic and Pacific all the year. We have the most diversified occupations; we have everything that makes for a great country. Let us give our best to this country in the way of legislation, not for selfish or political reasons, not for one section as against the other, not for one calling as against the other, but for Canada

Canada, the fairest of the dominions that form the British Empire, that Empire to which we as loyal Canadians are proud to belong.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. D. F. DRUMMOND (West Middlesex) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on the budget mainly because it has been said during the past two sessions that the Progressive members from Ontario seem to be very little interested in the tariff matters which are brought up in this House. But before saying anything about the budget, or other questions I want to refer, briefly to a resolution which it was my privilege to move this session regarding the marking of woollen goods. The resolution was opposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, referring to me said "What he is asking for is in the last analysis the highest degree of protection." Now, I have been of the opinion that it was beyond the dignity of any minister of the Crown to impute to any member of this House motives which were not contained in the resolution moved by me and which were not implied by one single word that I had uttered. If it is necessary for me-for the information of the House or for the information of the country, to state my position on protection I am ready to do so. It is my firm and honest belief that any system of protection which saps the very life blood from one basic industry for the purpose of building any other is economically and fundamentally wrong.
Members of all parties in this House join together in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) upon presenting his seventeenth budget. But there are some of us who are not so anxious to compliment him upon what that budget contains. During the last session, and also during the present one, I have been much amused at the taunt which has been flung across the House first from one side and then from the other -I must admit not so much from the government side as from the Conservative side- of repeated violation and breaking of promises made to the electors before the election. If my recollection serves me right, and I can go back a good many years, this peculiarity, if peculiarity you call it, is not confined to

The Budget-Mr. Drummond
one political sect. It may be that one party have been greater sinners than the other; but I think we can safely say that both, at one time or another in their career, have committed the same sin.
It has been said here during the present session that the measure of prosperity which the country enjoyed in 1896 and for some years after was due to the policy which had been adopted-I cannot say inaugurated- by the late Sir ^Vilfrid Laurier and his government. Looking back in our history we find that the Liberal party fought every election on the issue of protection from 1878 to 1896. That fact is very vividly imprinted upon my mind. I well remember some of those elections and the issue that was before the electors on those occasions. At one election the issue was free trade as they have it in England. At another it was unrestricted reciprocity. Again it was a tariff for revenue only; until we come to the time when the change of government occurred in 1896. I well remember that the tariff question was not an issue in that election. That contest was fought entirely uopn the Manitoba School question, and after the Liberal party got into power they were blamed-I think rightly blamed-for robbing the Conservative party of their much loved protection policy.
I now wish to refer for a moment to a part of a speech that was made by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). You will find it on page 2852 of Hansard of the present session. In that speech the hon. member made the following statement:
Perhaps it may shock some members on this side of the House-
I was greatly surprised to hear any hon. gentleman on that side of the House make the statement-
-when I say that I have very little confidence in the making of platforms, anyway. I do not believe that a government or members elected to the responsibility of a seat in this House should necessarily be asked to accept what may be ill-digested planks in any platform imposed upon them by people who come from various parts of the country and whose suggestions probably are as much dictated by political expediency as anything else; I do not believe that men who represent the public should be expected to carry out such ill-considered behests on the floor of this House. So that speaking for myself, Sir, I would say frankly that in the public interest the platform of 1919 should not be permitted to shackle the government responsible to all the people, whether it be a matter of tariff or anything else.
I want to ask, as briefly as I possibly can, that if the sentiment expressed in the foregoing extract from the hon. gentleman's speech is going to prevail in the public life of this

country what is going to become of political honour? If there is one thing more than another upon which the people of this country depend at the time of an election it is upon the principles that are advocated, upon the policy that is laid down by a political party, and which they say they intend to follow if put into power. It seems to me that the statement I have quoted is one that would drag the honour of any political party in the mire.
I now wish to make reference to an utterance by the Prime Minister before the. last election. Speaking at Bolton on the 29th October, 1921, as reported in the Toronto Globe, he said:
I believe in doing all possible to further the legitimate interests of agriculture, as such a policy was going to help all industries in Canada. The Liberals did not propose to continue to help a few men to become multi-millionaires.
He went on further to say that he was in favour of the most drastic measures of economy, and retrenchment in every direction. No voice rang out with louder denunciations throughout the land, no voice gave a greater promise of economy, than that of the present Prime Minister. No statesman before the last election made, with greater emphasis, promises of retrenchment than the leader of the government to-day; and when declared successful at the polls he boastingly heralded the dawn of a new era that would speedily put the country upon its feet financially and cure all the ills that are in every case the aftermath of war. But two years have gone by, and notwithstanding the repeated protests of the Farmers' party for economy and some legislation that would be of assistance in remedying the grievances which they complained of, and which were undoubtedly real, the same need for economy exists to-day and their grievances remain unredressed.
I do not want to be partisan, because that is one of the greatest crimes any Progressive could be guilty of, but I wish to refer for a moment to something that took place in the Conservative party which I hope will prove the assertions I have made that pledges and promises have been violated by both parties in the past. In the year 1911 the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), speaking in favour of a reduction of the duty upon agricultural implements said, Hanasard page 1917:
But the charge I have to make, and which I hope to bring home to the government this afternoon, is not that one though it is the most serious,-

The Budget-Mr. Drummond
That is the one that they have made false
pretences.
-but it is this that in their attempts to continue the National Policy which had obtained for years before, they have overlooked, they have neglected one essential feature of that policy, they have quite forgotten its guiding principle, namely the principle that as our industrial institutions advanced in strength, as they were able with every advance to acquire a hold of the home market, the import duties were to be diminished and adjusted in order to meet the evolving and changing conditions.
Then follows the wonderful statement made in that speech that the government then in power had helped themselves into power by maintaining themselves behind ramparts of gold.
Also in the same Hansard and at page 1919 the present leader of the Opposition stated:
As everybody knows in 1896, and for two years previously, the duty on agricultural implements of all *kinds stood at 20 per cent and the same rate of duty was maintained by this government for eleven years subsequently, or until 1907. In the meantime the insidious work of the officials of this government in increasing the valuation for duty had got into play, and while the nominal duty was maintained at 20 per cent, the actual duty was very seriously increased. . . Other regulations were made by the government which afforded the manufacturer a greater protection than the 20 per cent set out in the Customs Act would indicate.
Now to prove the assertion that the Conservatives after having obtained power in 1911 did the very same thing they charged the Liberals with doing, I quote the following figures obtained from the Bureau of Statistics regarding the duty on agricultural implements from 1912 to 1915, and the duty on the same implements in the year 1921, the last year in which they held office. It is not necess-sary to go through the whole list of agricultural implements, and for briefness I will take binders. The duty on binders in 1915 under the 174 per cent tariff was $18.96. I may say just here that this is to some extent at least an answer to the question that was asked the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. King) by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Sinclair) on Friday, I think. The duty in 1915, under the 174 per cent tariff was $18.96, according to the information furnished by the Bureau of Statistics for the year 1919. The valuation for duty purposes of that binder was $108.35. In the year 1921 the valuation on the binder for duty purposes was $182.60 and under the reduction which they boasted of from 174 to 124 per cent the agriculturist who bought the binder was obliged to pay in protective tariff the sum of $22.82.
Could the hon. member give us the tariff under the reciprocity ^arrangement of 1911?

Twenty per cent reduced to 174 per cent, and in 1915 or 1916 it was reduced to 124 per cent. Now again let me make reference to the home markets that have been boasted of by some of those who are in favour of a protective tariff. Those who stand committed to a protective tariff as being in the best interests of the people of Canada are fond of boasting that the home market is provided by the industries which are brought into existence or kept in existence by that protective tariff.
In that connection I want to quote a few figures which are also obtained from a report of the Bureau of Statistics issued in 1920, and giving the statistics for the year 1919:
Number of implement manufacturers in Canada in 1919, 86.
Total capital invested in implement manufacturing
industries, $83,276,450.
Total value of products of said implements manufactured in Canada during that year, $37,715,331.
According to this report there was exported from Canada in 1919, $8,831,803 worth of manufactures, leaving a balance which was either purchased by the agricultural people of Canada, or retained in stock to the value ol $28,883,528. That was the amount of goods left over after $8,000,000 worth had been exported. While the average duty at that time was 124 per cent, under the tariff introduced by the government last session, the protective duty upon agricultural implements was reduced by 24 per cent, which was boastingiy held up as something that the Progressives should be eternally thankful for, we will therefore strike 10 per cent as the average duty. Ten per cent upon the sum of $28,882,528 means that the Canadian agriculturists who bought those implements paid in duty t to the manufactured industries of the Dominion of Canada the sum of $2,888,352.80.
Now the number of men employed in the agricultural implement factories of Canada in that year was 10,808 and the wages paid 'o those employees was $11,715,331, or an average salary per employee of $1,084. If you will divide the number of employees, 10,808, into the total amount that the users of agricultural implements in Canada were required to pay in duty, you get the sum of $265.80, which is the amount that it cost the purchasers of agricultural implements for each employee who weis engaged in the manufacture of these implements, or in other words, the Canadian agriculturist who purchases implements is charged $265.80 for each employee for the home market which such employee provides.
I will leave hon. members to draw their own conclusions as to whether every employee in the implement manufacturing companies is



The Budget-Mr. Drummond
worth $265 to the agricultural people of this Dominion.
I wish to say a word or two about the Canadian National Railways. While I am one of those who would wish to see the Canadian National Railways placed upon a basis that would avoid a deficit, I cannot undei-stand how such a thing is going to happen when we have such instances as the Chateau Laurier, one of the Canadian National's own hotels here in the city of Ottawa showing an annual deficit of $351,000. If that is the basis upon which our National Railways are going to pay, it will be a long time before we ever reach the desired end. From the report that was given, the hotels in the other parts of the system also show large deficits.
What is the deficit in connection with the Chateau Laurier? I did not catch the figure?

The figure given to me was $351,000 for the Chateau Laurier, and I am led to believe that that is correct.
Some members in the two old political parties have lovingly spoken of the Progressive party, but they have not chosen just the right words to give expression to their love. As nearly as I can remember, this was started by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) before the last election. The leader of the Opposition in his manifesto published before the election of 1921,-and you will find this in all the papers of that period- after referring to the policy of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), used these words:
But a stronger and more menacing enemy has arisen. For some years past there has been growing up, first on the prairies of the West, and later through selected parts of eastern Canada, a party backed by a costly and persistent propaganda, the purpose of which is to reverse the tariff policy of this country.
I should like to ask my right hon. friend, who, I am sorry to see, is not in his seat to-night:	Whom is the Progressive party
menacing? Whom are they the enemy of? If there is any degree of citizenship, those at present engged in the pursuit of agriculture are the most distinguished of any. They are the men and the women on whom the hope of the future of Canada depends. They are the men and the women who must be depended upon to fill cars for their precious railways and precious merchant marine which are standing monuments of the want of foresight of both the old political parties. They are the people above all others who, if they moved away, would leave Canada bankrupt.
Looking at the matter from the standpoint of what has been attained or what has been

received by the occupation of agriculture from any government that has ever sat on the treasury benches of this House, I do not think there should be any doubt in anyone's mind as to the reasons why sixty-five Progressive members were elected at the last election. Perhaps I should correct myself a little as regards those sixty-five, because by a natural process of elimination known as the survival of the fittest, we have been reduced to sixty-three. But I think I am safe in saying, as regards those sixty-three, that notwithstanding the fact that we have not received very much yet, we who form the Progressive party will still continue to go forward and onward, firm in the belief and strong in the hope that there is somewhere in the distance, be it far or near, a hill top radiant with the sunshine of something for the agricultural people, a hill top radiant with the glory of equal opportunity to all and special privileges to none.
Mr. DAVID SPENCE tParkdale): Mr. Speaker, talking seems to be catching; my hon. friends all around have been talking; but I do not intend to cover the whole country from Vancouver to Plalifax, nor to make any lengthy speech. While representing one of the largest ridings in Canada, I may say the second or third largest, unlike my hon. friends to my left, I have no complaints to make; I am at peace with all the world. My riding is asking for nothing; it expects nothing, and it will get nothing. Anything the government can pass over to my hon. friends from the prairie provinces, let them hand it over to them to appease their hunger.
I hesitate in rising to-night to say very much after what has been said so ably by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me. I must confess that I am not an orator, and I hjve never developed my oratorical powers. My life has been a busy one in the business world, and I am trying my best to give service to the people who entrust their business to me, so that speaking has not been my forte. When I entered Parliament I expected to meet big men discussing big things; instead, I find one-half of our time wasted discussing erratic resolutions and economic questions which are of no account whatever.
I want to make some observations, from a business man's standpoint, with reference to certain things in connection with this parliament, and if I err or get out of order, I hope you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker. I do not intend to discuss the budget at any length other than to say that I cannot support the amendment to the budget, because

The Budget-Mr. Spence
it means a lowering of the tariff and possibly, free trade. I do not intend to support the budget itself, because reference has been made in it to reciprocity. In my humble opinion, the producers of the soil in this country cannot compete with our friends to the south of us, particularly as regards fruit and vegetables-and I have a long experience in those lines-on account of climatic conditions and the extensive markets to the south as compared with climatic conditions in this country, which are much colder, so that more energy and everything else are required in order to produce our stuff. Are hon. members aware that from Florida to North and South Carolina, truck gardeners can raise from two to three crops a year? That cannot be done in Canada. Take the eastern shore of Virginia alone, the greatest producing country on this continent, particularly in potatoes, where they have thousands of acres of potatoes raised by a co-operative organization that supplies the greatest part of the United States and this country during the latter part of May, June and July. After that, we have invariably sold them our old Ontario potatoes, and they replant another crop for their home market in the winter months with great success. Can that be done in Canada? I say, no. I am in favour of more protection for the tiller of the soil, apart altogether from any question of the manul/acturing industries of the country. Why should the ingredients that go to the manufacture of oleomargarine, or why should oleomargarine itself, come into this country without paying a duty? I do not know whether or not there is a slight duty on oleomargarine, but at any rate I would put a tariff on these products equal to the Fordney tariff on similar Canadian products.
One hundred per cent.

I beg your pardon? I did not hear what the hon. member said. However, I want to assure my hon. friends to my left that they have my sincere sympathy in their difficulties. But they cannot expect to bring about an improvement in their conditions without some sacrifice on their part, such as the business men have had to make in the past few years since the close of the Great War. I would suggest to those hon. gentlemen that they stick more closely to their business. I would advise them to remain on their farms and exercise a continuous supervision over them just as the business men of this country have to do in connection with their various enterprises. That after all is mi	<
the only way in which any business can succeed; and if that is done in connection with the farms of the West I think that my good friends will make a great success of their farming. In any event, we wish them luck and prosperity.
It gives me much pleasure to compliment the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) on the optimism he displayed in the course of his speech the other day in his discussion of matters in the West. I think that speeches of that kind go to inspire confidence in the people and help to build up the country; it is that kind of speech that we need, which is very different from the calamity howling that we have been hearing from our hon. friends to the left, who have been talking of secession and things of that sort that cannot but be detrimental to the interests of the country. Those hon. gentlemen seem to me to be troubled with "imaginitis." They seem to think that the members in this parliament from the East are not sympathetically disposed to them. Let me assure my hon. friends that that is not so; I want them to believe that they have our deepest sympathy and that we are willing to make any sacrifice that we possibly can to improve things so far as they are concerned. One hon. gentleman the other evening in his speech, after complaining of everything conceivable, made this statement: "If we cannot get along together, let us part good friends." I do not take that view of things at all; I say that we must get along together not only in the interests of Canada, but because I am sure we all have the welfare of the Empire at heart. Let us determine that there shall be no secession. Another hon. gentleman to my left, after threatening parliament with every imaginable ill, said that if we did not listen to his groans and cries we might have reason to regret it. This is what he said, and it is something that in my opinion should not be tolerated in this House of Commons:
Hon. members may not believe this; -*
I may say, we had not the impression before, but what I am about to read would, if possible, confirm it if it did exist:
-some hon. members are inclined to laugh and say: "Oh, the agriculturists are always whining," but if hon. members keep on saying that, I assure them that they are taking a dangerous course. We may not always whine. We have in this country a strong foreign element, and sometimes it is necessary to keep them in curb. If the House and the country continue to take that attitude, an attitude of, as I said before, cold-blooded insolence, we may come to a time when there will be more unrest and more real trouble than we have had in the past. I would just give hon. members fair warning. Hon. members may laugh at this if they like; but that will be the effect.
The Budget-Mr. Spence

Now, speeches of that kind are positively detrimental to this fair country and should be discouraged, at least on the floor of the House. Let me tell my good friends to my left that they know nothing to-day about hard times. Let them go back to the days between 1892 and 1897 when pork sold at 3\ cents to 4 cents per pound, eggs from 8 to 10 cents, butter from 10 to 12 cents, and beef at any old price; when geese sold at from 3 to 5 cents a pound, turkey from 7 to 8 cents a pound, and when there was scarcely any demand for chickens, these being from 15 to 20 cents per pair, with potatoes at 10 cents a bag. I can substantiate every statement I make in this connection, because I bought all these commodities in those days.
And I sold them.
Yes, and I sympathize with you; and if you keep on talking in the strain in which you are talking to-day you will soon bring back the conditions that existed then.
But sympathy is not worth much; what would you do?

We have been doing everything for you. I know conditions in the West just as well as my hon. friends do, for I have covered the prairie provinces. I have travelled all over this country from Halifax to Vancouver and Victoria, and I can say that the conditions in the country from which my hon. friends come were no worse in those days than were the conditions in our part of the country, nor indeed, were they half as bad. I remember that at the same time bread sold at 4 to 5 cents a large loaf retail; I sold tons pf it myself.
A loaf of bread and quart of whiskey would be a cheap meal.
What would wheat and oats be worth at that time?
We ought to know; we were selling wheat in those days you speak of.

Then why do you forget those bad times so soon? The life of the farmer, I think, has improved a lot since those days with a few exceptions, and this is due to the activities of the Department of Agriculture under different governments, that department having improved dairying and farming generally. The Agricultural department under every government has done a great deal for hon. gentlemen. It has established cold storages, while private interests have also built similar institutions, enabling the speculator to pay these gentlemen and

those whom they represent a reasonable price for their butter, their eggs, their poultry and hogs during the summer season, when the amount of these products coming in could not possibly be consumed. And yet hon. gentlemen growl about not having accommodation, and so forth.
Mr. Speaker-
Pardon me; I am talking now. When I get through with this sentence you may interrupt me.
I will not bother you any more, I am sure.

Butter especially has been improved to the greatest extent. I remember well having seen dozens upon dozens, nay, hundreds of barrels, come into our market, some of which was absolutely unfit for food; and when we segregated the good from the bad and got all we could for the best, we had to sell the rest at from 4 to 5 cents i pound. To-day, through the good offices of the departments of agriculture of the provinces there is no excuse for there being any bad butter in the country, and the lady who cannot make good butter nowadays can sell her milk to the creamery or take it to the cheese factory. What else do hon. gentlemen want to have done for them? To-day, I am glad to say, there is a big 12 m. demand for the woman who can make her own butter. In the fall of the year when the farmers decide to get lid of their stock before the winter season sets in, for one reason or another, generally to obviate feeding during the winter, veiy heavy shipments come in and the cold storage is again brought into use to save the situation. These gentlemen bitterly complain because they cannot get the prices they want for their stock. But how would it be possible to consume trainloads of half-fed cattle, the scrubs that come into the cities and large centres? How would it be possible at all to make any use of them without cold storages? Again, my good friends are protected by the provision that has been made for them in the different provinces.
There are too many people to-day who know everybody else's business but their own. Before entering public life men should have a broad knowledge of their country's needs as a whole and not think their own little part of the country alone needs attention. Thank goodness I have never been that way. All my life I have tried to give the other fellow the best of the deal. When in 1909 I first offered myself as a candidate for the city council of Toronto my wide experience on the water-

The Budget-Mr. Spence
front made me realize the necessity and importance of water-borne transportation, and I advocated then, as I do now, the deepening of the waterway between Montreal and Toronto and also the deepening of the Wel-lan canal. I pictured ocean boats leaving Toronto loaded with apples and other merchandise for the Liverpool and Glasgow markets and bringing back return cargoes for delivery clear to the head of the lakes. Can any hon. gentleman tell me that such a waterborne traffic would not build up the central and western provinces? And yet I have heard some hon. members from the West ridiculing the idea of a deep waterway to Montreal. The day is not far distant I think when we shall see the realization of this idea which will mean so much to Canada and the Empire.
The Ontario cabinet has been accused of irresponsible	government-government	by
commission. As I see this administration it is a case of government by committee. The government has refused to accept responsibility for any important legislation introduced this session. The government is run like a six-ring circus-committees sitting in every quarter at a cost to the country in the neighborhood of $500,000, with little prospect of any return commensurate with this outlay. We have been told by the Prime Minister that we are to have a fair and equitable redistribution. Well, on the committee to which the redistribution bill has been assigned we have ten members of the Liberal party, five of the Progressive party and four of the Conservative party. Do you expect to get a fair and equitable redistribution from such a committee? I say. no.
I am not going to criticize the budget too severely. I am glad to see that the tax has been changed on soft drinks and that the cigarette duty has been reduced to its old figure. I wrote a letter last year to the Minister of Finance pointing out just what would happen in respect to the increased duties he then placed on these two articles. I received a very nice answer from him in which he said he would take my suggestions into his very serious consideration-that is what Sir Oliver Mowat used to say-but I do not think he did. However, he has taken my advice at last. Speaking of the income tax, I think the penalties are entirely too high. A friend of mine who was executor of a small Toronto estate forgot to make his return within the specified time, but he did so three days later and paid the tax. In the meantime the income tax department saw fit to fine him $50. Now, could he take that out of the widow's mite? No, he had to take it out of his own
pocket. That is penalizing a good, respectable citizen and I say the law should be changed to prevent the repetition of such an injustice.
We should know to-day whether the Post Office Department is being run at a profit or a loss. The sale of postage stamps to-day is enormous. Many of these stamps are placed on cheques and receipts and go to the credit of the Post Office Department. Altogether it is a very badly managed affair. Then the reduction of the maximum stamp on cheques is no help to the ordinary man of business. A wholesale man like myself has occasion to draw many cheques from $100 up to $2,000 or $3,000, and consequently the reduction only benefits bankers, brokers and millionaires. The rate of duty on cheques is extremely high and eats up our profits. There is not a dollar you make that somebody is not trying to get it.
If the hon. Minister of Finance were in his seat I would ask him why was the sales tax taken off newsprint. To my mind it was not taken off in the interests of the Progressive party or of the consuming public; it was bribery pure and simple to get the support of the newspapers of the country. Furthermore, there is no class of business to-day that can afford to pay a 6 per cent sales tax. To my mind some commodities to-day that are free from duty could well afford to stand a tax, and it would be a good way of getting revenue. Take bananas alone, for some reason or other the banana trust, composed of the foreign element of this country and the United States, control our politicians and consequently not a cent of duty has ever been placed on bananas. Bananas to the value of $5,210,000 were imported last year. There is absolutely no reason in the world why a moderate duty should not be imposed on bananas, especially as there is nothing so detrimental to our fruit growers as the importation and sale of bananas in the months of June, July, August and September when our own strawberries, plums, peaches and other fruits come on the market. Oranges and pineapples are free of duty. I am not advocating that they should be made dutiable, I merely mention that they enter free. Grape fruit for some reason or other is taxed too high, one cent a pound being equivalent to seventy or eighty cents a box. Ten times the amount of money would come into the Treasury if grape fruit, oranges, lemons, and pineapples were taxed 25 cents a box, and this tax would never be noticed in the resale price.
If there is any commission in this world that should be appointed-I do not advocate

commissions because I believe the men who are elected to this House should bear the responsibility of legislating for this country- but if there is any commission that should be appointed it is a tariff commission, composed of men who know something about trade conditions in this country, instead of this parliament tampering with the tariff from time to time. The day after the Minister of Finance delievered his budget I read in a Toronto morning paper-I was not able to be here on that day-that the tariff on potatoes had been increased from twenty cents to thirty-five cents per hundred. The public thought that was an awful increase. I do not think it meant from twenty to thirty-five cents a hundred, because the duty was 20 cents per bushel. It was only increasing the duty one and two-thirds cents per hundred pounds, and I do not think the tariff should be interfered with to make a little change like that. Again, we have established the principle of a certain sized barrel, two and a half bushels, or two and three-quarters, or three bushels. To-day we are fighting with the customs officials all the time over the weight of the barrel, and I say it is not worth disturbing trade for such a small amount. I think it is easier collecting duty than anything else, and that would be my system of raising money and having less taxation, but I would recommend strongly to any government that is in power in this country not to make these small changes in the tariff, but appoint a tariff commission composed of men who know the business needs of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I have the sympathy of every hon. gentleman in this House because on some occasion, whether it was last year, five years, ten years ago, thirty or even forty years ago every hon. gentleman has been in the position in which I find myself at this moment. It is a wonderful thing for a man to have the record of forty years in the House of Commons which I believe two hon. members of this House enjoy, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister or Railways (Mr. Graham). But it is a more wonderful thing to be forty years in the Canadian House of Commons and have the respect and love of the entire House.
Mr. Speaker, when a member comes to the House of Commons for the first time, he comes here as you know with just the vision of his own little constituency. He does not just at first get the vision of the Dominion of Canada, or, as I suppose he will later on, the

vision of Canada as a nation, the world's vision, for we all believe that Canada is a nation in the building. We believe the day will come when we shall have countless thousands of people in this country to develop the resources that have been bestowed upon us with such a bounteous hand, but just at first all we can do in our maiden effort is to talk about the things back home. All governments say, if they are asked to do anything out of the ordinary: We must first feel the pulse of the people, so I would like for a few minutes to present the pulse of my constituency.
I represent a constituency in the centre of Saskatchewan, in that great granary that is called the bread basket of the Empire. Every year the milling companies of the West just after threshing time send out and get samples of all grains in the different parts of the West and submit it to the baking and milling tests, and when they find the grain that is best adapted for milling they send to that particular district and get that wheat for their mills. The wheat in the northern part of my constituency-it is an old settled district for forty years-has been selected as the wheat the millers want to grind in their own mill. Now we do not get any premium on that.
I say it is an old-settled district, and one of the best. The southern part of the riding is a newer district where some of my people are forty miles from a railroad, but it is a good district, and I was glad to note from the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) the other day that we are going to have a railroad there. Half of my constituents are rural and half of them are urban, and I make no apologies to my urban constituents for discussing the problems of the rural people, for in the West, in the farming district on the prairie, the interest of the city is so connected with that of the farmer that they cannot be divided. We have only two classes of people in that country, the people who can make a living on the farm and make a fair living, and the people who are enabled to live in the city because the farmer makes a fair living. In the early days the farmers were fairly successful before the war and we got a city, but now that the farmers are not doing well their condition is reflected in the city, and I want to say to you that these are strenuous days in western Canada, and I fancy there are going to be strenuous days all over Canada because when the buying power of the farmer is diminished it is reflected in the business of the whole country. Canada was started by a little colony of farmers, and though our commerce has ex-

The Budget-Mr. McKUlop
paneled it still remains true that the great industry of this country is agriculture. We in the West have always believed that a high tariff bore unduly heavily on the West.
Let me put it in another way. We will suppose, if you can imagine it, that in place of having the great Dominion of Canada we had an eastern Canada and a western Canada, that these were both British possessions but divided into two separate provinces, and that the people of eastern Canada came to the people of western Canada and said: Let us form a great confederation and have one great Canada. If you will form that confederation we will make this proposition to you. Remember that we have the great bulk of the population east of the great lakes, and consequently we will have the voting power and will make the laws. But we will make this proposition to you: If you will join us in the East we will put a high tariff on all the things you consume. You will be allowed to take all your products of the farm and sell them in the markets of the world in competition with the whole world, but we will put a heavy duty on everything you buy, on your implements, on your clothing, on your boots and shoes. Yes, we will do more than that. We will take your lands, your mines, and administer them for you.
Do you think that would have a tendenev to make the West join with the East? I do not think it would. A good many gentleman here seem to think that we are on the up grade, that we have crossed the Rubicon and are going to climb up. I hope that is the case but I do not think so. Some of the brightest minds in the world to-day belie''e that the best way to have a reconstruction would be for the different nations to cancel their debts and commence again. The wav has been over for a good many years and in my opinion we have not started re-construction yet. Re-construction means to commence at the bottom and build up from the foundation. The only way you will build a permanent structure in Canada is to take a recapitalization of your debts and then adjust those debts. There are thousands of people in western Canada to-day who are adjusting their debts-the debtor and the creditor-and starting anew. We will never accomplish what wc want in this country, in my humble opinion, until we adjust our debts as between the debtor and the creditor. This Canada of ours has lost millions of money during the war, and the trouble is that to-day some people want to make others bear more than their share of that- loss. When our people bear their proportionate share of the burden then
we will be able to build afresh; and it is a duty of parliament, I think, to do for the people what they are unable to do for themselves. That is to make every Canadian, as far as is possible, bear his share of the burden. When every Canadian realizes his responsibility and is willing to do his part then we shall really commence to build up the country.
Mr. HUGH C. McKILLOP (West Elgin):
I am sure the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) must be tired of the congratulations which have been showered upon him from every comer of the chamber and therefore I will content myself with wishing him for the future many years of good health and happiness and freedom from parliamentary duties.
The budget as brought down this year does not display very many changes as compared with the previous budget. True there are a number of small changes. For example, the tariff is reduced on sugar but at the same time it is increased on clothing, so that in the end it works out very much the same. It is just about the same old tariff. Some items are higher, some are lower, but on the whole it is just about the same. This is the second budget that has been brought down by the present government, and it makes one wonder whether they have forgotten altogether the platform they adopted in 1919, which was broadcasted in blazing colours all over this country. Take even their more recent pre-election promises which they made throughout this country in 1921. So far there have not been such changes in the tariff as to give very much encouragement to those who supported them in the last election. It is no wonder, therefore, that the present government have not achieved greater success in the by-elections that have taken place since they came into power. Mr. Speaker, the handwriting is on the wall, warning the present government that unless they change their ways and endeavour to carry out some of their promises their time in office is going to be very short.
Now, I want to direct attention for a few moments to a matter that concerns the bean producers of this country, and in dealing with this subject I will present the facts as briefly as possible. For a number of years past the duty on beans imported into Canada has been 25 cents a bushel while beans entering the United States from Canada have to meet a duty of $1.20 a bushel. I claim that this is not right, and that it constitutes a hardship on the farmers of Canada who have been engaged in the production of beans. Since this condition has prevailed many farmers have been driven out of the industry, while others have so curtailed their production that not over

The Budget-Mr. McKillop
40 per cent of the quantity of beans that used to be grown in Canada is now produced in this country. Take in the period from 1892 to 1901 the production of beans in Canada amounted to 875,597 bushels. In the latter year the import of beans amounted to 11,003 bushels. Since that time imports of beans have grown by leaps and bounds and at the same time the home production has steadily declined. To such an extent has that been the case that in the year 1920-the last period for which I have figures-the Canadian bean production reached a total of only 388,499 bushels, whereas in the same time the imports had grown to the extent of 444,698 bushels. In 1920 we find the production of beans in Canada was only a little over one-third as much as it was during the ten years that I have mentioned. What is the cause of this? Simply that owing to the low tariff maintained by Canada this country has been made a dumping ground by the nation to the south of us. This is not as it should be, and no self-respecting government should allow such a condition to continue any longer. Then there are other countries. For instance, Austria and Japan send a lot of beans into this country. I do not think it is fair, equitable or just that the farmers of Canada should be called upon to compete with countries where the standard of living is so much lower and where labour is so muoh cheaper. I have it on good authority that a labourer in Japan does not receive as muoh in the fields for two weeks' work as the labourer does in this country for one day's work. Now, Mr. Speaker, I claim that if this duty on beans coming into this country were put where it should be, and the bean producers given to understand that the home market was available to them, it would only be a matter of a short time when the production of beans in Canada would far exceed any production of the past. It is suggested that the reason the tariff is kept down is to favour the consumer. As to that I will only say that, with all the importations of beans in the past, the consumer is not buying the bean a particle cheaper than he did two years ago, as it is a well known fact that for years the price of beans in small quantities has been ten cents per pound. I am convinced that if the tariff on this commodity is raised the consumer will not have to pay any more than at present, as the production of beans would so increase as to keep the price to the consumer where it is at present or even lower. I hope the government will give this matter their earnest 
attention and see that the farmers and bean producers have a fair show.
I should like to draw the attention of the House for a few moments to the conditions of the workingmen in this country. We have at present on our statutes, under the Department of Labour, what is known as fair wage officers, and I understand that one of these officers is stationed in Montreal, another in Ottawa, another in Toronto, another in Winnipeg and another in Vancouver. I would have these officers inquire in their respective districts as to the condition under which the workingman is labouring, first as to wages, and secondly, as to the cost of living in his community. It is a well-known fact you may have a labouring man in one place who is doing a certain kind of work and receiving what is termed a living wage, and at the same time you may have, a thousand miles from him, a man engaged in similar work, receiving the same wage, and yet, on account of the high cost of living, hardly able to make ends meet. I claim it should be the duty of the fair wage officer to inquire into the workingman's conditions and to see that he is satisfied and contented, for after all, a satisfied and contented workingman is one of Canada's greatest assets.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I claim that if the workingmen are contented, a great obstacle is placed in the way of the entrance into Canada of Bolshevism. For my part, I have no use for Bolshevists, or Bolshevism, or of any other kind of "ism" except good, sound, strong, loyal Canadianism. I am satisfied that 90 per cent of our working men belong to that class. I do not wish to be misunderstood in this matter. I do not hold any brief for any radical element. The class I am speaking for is the honest, sincere and loyal workingman, the man who wants to give an honest day's work for an honest day's pay. I want to be placed on record as being ready, at any time while a member of this House, to suport any sane legislation that has for its object the bettering of the workingman's conditions.
In conclusion, I may say that since coming to this House I have heard a good deal of talk about low tariff, and a great deal of talk about free trade, but I am convinced that neither one of these will ever cure the ills Canada is suffering from. On the other hand, I am just as strongly convinced that what this country needs is a strong national policy, if she is ever going to take the place that she originally intended to take, as one of the leading nations of the world.
